title: I've been to the Netherlands
goal: Choose between *hebben* and *zijn* as the helper verb, and use the simple past for the most common verbs.
bekal: knowing when a past sentence takes *ben* instead of *heb*
wave: Go back to **unit 17**: retell your yesterday in ten past-tense sentences, this time each one opening with a time expression.

dialogs.title: Dialog — Bij de kapper
dialogs.intro: Dutch barbers are famously chatty. Budi is stuck in twenty minutes of conversation — and it turns out to be the best practice he gets all month.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nee, ik ben in Bandung geboren. Ik ben hier sinds januari.
lines.id: No, I was born in Bandung. I've been here since January.
lines.literal: no, I am in Bandung born. I am here since January.

lines.speaker: Kapper:
lines.id: So? Do you like it here?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Het was moeilijk in het begin. Het weer was verschrikkelijk.
lines.id: It was hard at first. The weather was terrible.
lines.literal: it was hard in the beginning. the weather was terrible.

lines.speaker: Kapper:
lines.text: Ha! Dat is het altijd. En nu?
lines.id: Ha! It always is. And now?
lines.literal: ha! that is it always. and now?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nu gaat het goed. Ik ben naar veel steden geweest.
lines.id: Now it's going well. I've been to lots of cities.
lines.literal: now goes it well. I am to many cities been.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ik ben in Rotterdam, Den Haag en Maastricht geweest.
lines.id: I've been to Rotterdam, The Hague, and Maastricht.
lines.literal: I am in Rotterdam, The-Hague and Maastricht been.

lines.speaker: Kapper:
lines.text: Maastricht! Daar ben ik nog nooit geweest.
lines.id: Maastricht! I've never even been there.
lines.literal: there am I still never been.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Echt? Het is drie uur met de trein.
lines.id: Really? It's three hours by train.
lines.literal: really? that is three hours with the train.

lines.speaker: Kapper:
lines.text: Precies. Dat is ver, hoor. Ik ben ooit in Zeeland geweest.
lines.id: Exactly. That's far, you know. I did go to Zeeland once.
lines.literal: precisely. that is far, hoor. I am ever in Zeeland been.

notes: **Ben je hier geboren?** — *geboren zijn* (to be born) always takes *zijn*, just like English "I was born". You'll be asked this sentence many times.
**Ik ben hier sinds januari** — *sinds* (since) takes the **present**, not the past. Dutch says "I am here since January", where English says "I have been here since…".
**Bevalt het?** — from *bevallen* (to please, suit). The classic question for newcomers: "do you like it here?". The answer: *Ja, het bevalt me goed.*
**Het was moeilijk** — *was* is the simple past of *zijn*. For *zijn*, *hebben*, and the modal verbs, this is the everyday form, not the *ge-* form.

**Ik ben naar veel steden geweest** — note *ben*, not *heb*: *zijn* is used for moving from place to place and for change of state. And *geweest* is used for "have been to", not *gegaan* — exactly as in English.
**Daar ben ik nog nooit geweest** — "I've never been there". The order: place expression first, helper verb second, participle at the end.
**Ik ben ooit in Zeeland geweest** — *ooit* means "ever, at some point". Don't confuse it with *nooit* (never) and *altijd* (always).

**Dat is ver, hoor** — and this is no joke. The Netherlands is small, yet a two-hour trip already counts as far. For someone like Budi, used to overnight bus rides at home, it's one of the funniest cultural differences.

grammars.title: Hebben or zijn?
body: Most verbs take *hebben*. The ones that take *zijn* are a small group with one common thread: **movement or change**.
after: ⚠️ Some verbs of motion can take either, depending on whether there's a destination: *Ik **heb** gefietst* (I cycled — the activity) versus *Ik **ben** naar Utrecht gefietst* (I cycled to Utrecht — the movement). Same for *lopen*, *rijden*, *zwemmen*, *vliegen*.
*Zijn* + *geweest* replaces *gegaan* for experiences: *Ik ben in Maastricht geweest* (I've been to Maastricht) versus *Ik ben naar Maastricht gegaan* (I went off to Maastricht).
When in doubt: almost every verb with a direct object takes *hebben*. *Ik heb een boek gelezen*, *ik heb koffie gedronken*.

grammars.title: The everyday simple past
body: Dutch has two past forms. The one with *ge-* (units 17–18) is for conversation; this one, the *imperfectum*, is for **states**, for **longer stories**, and — most importantly — for a group of verbs that sound odd in the other form.
after: For these twelve verbs, the *imperfectum* is used **far more often** than the *ge-* form. The Dutch say *ik was moe*, not *ik ben moe geweest*; *ik moest werken*, not *ik heb moeten werken*.

For other verbs, use the unit 17–18 form in conversation. The *imperfectum* of ordinary verbs (*ik werkte*, *ik fietste*) shows up mostly in writing and stories — you'll read it far more often than you say it.
The form: weak verbs add **-te** or **-de** by the same 't kofschip rule: *werken → werkte*, *wonen → woonde*.

head: Nederlands
English
rows: Ben je wel eens in Amsterdam geweest?
Have you ever been to Amsterdam?
Ik ben er twee keer geweest.
Ik heb het nog nooit geprobeerd.
Dat heb ik nog nooit gehoord.
Ik ben nog nooit zo nat geworden.

blocks.text: *Wel eens* and *ooit* both mean "ever": *wel eens* is more casual and more common in everyday questions. The negative is always *nog nooit* (never yet), not *niet ooit*.

blocks.title: Provinces worth a visit
items: **Zeeland** — the delta and the giant *Deltawerken* dams, built after the 1953 flood.
**Friesland** — has its own language (*Frysk*), the Netherlands' second official language.
**Limburg** — hilly, and the only place in the Netherlands with a "mountain" (322 meters).
**Groningen** — the student city with the youngest average age in the country.
**Noord-Holland** — Amsterdam, Haarlem, and the windmill village of *Zaanse Schans*.
⚠️ For students, an **OV-chipkaart** with a weekend subscription puts the whole country within cheap reach.

sections.title: Telling a story in the past

blocks.text: See how the two past forms work side by side in one story — *was*, *had*, *moest* for states, and the *ge-* form for events:

head: Nederlands
English
rows: Ik moest om zes uur opstaan.
I had to get up at six.
Ik had geen tijd voor ontbijt.
I had no time for breakfast.
Daarna ben ik naar kantoor gefietst.
Then I cycled to the office.
On the way it started raining.
Maar mijn collega had koffie gezet.
But my colleague had made coffee.

blocks.text: This pattern — states with *was/had/moest*, events with *heb/ben + ge-* — is the most natural way to tell a story in spoken Dutch. If you can tell the story of one bad day like the one above, you've moved past A1.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with heb/heeft or ben/is.
Fill in the blanks with the simple past.
Put the words in the right order.
items: nooit / daar / ik / nog / ben / geweest

answers: ben — heb — is — heeft — zijn — is
was — had — moest — wist — zei — gingen
Ik ben in Rotterdam geweest. — Ik ben daar nog nooit geweest. — Ik ben in Bandung geboren. — Gisteren was het heel koud. — Ik heb de trein gemist. — Toen was alles weer goed.
Ik ben in Maastricht geweest. — Daar ben ik nog nooit geweest. — Gisteren was het koud. — Ik heb de trein gemist. — Ik ben in Bandung geboren.
